title: pg_trgm similarity, ICU collations and case-insensitive matching, unaccent
summary: pg_trgm scores strings by shared three-letter pieces: it forgives typos, not ş typed as s. An unaccent search key in an IMMUTABLE wrapper folds those away (merging ı and i), and nondeterministic ICU collations make =, LIKE and UNIQUE case-insensitive with Turkish rules.

examples.title: Trigrams, similarity, % and <->, on Turkish city names

annotations.note: pg_trgm is a trusted extension, so the non-superuser playground role may create it; the rollback removes it again.

Each word is lowercased, padded with two spaces in front and one behind, and cut into three-character pieces. The six entries for ığdır are its six trigrams; those containing non-ASCII letters print as hex codes. Which characters count as letters depends on the database's LC_CTYPE (see the pitfalls): with LC_CTYPE C, this database used to return only four trigrams, around d and r.

similarity is shared trigrams divided by all distinct trigrams of both strings: Antlya and Antalya share 5 of 10. % compares it with pg_trgm.similarity_threshold (default 0.3), and a trigram index can serve %.
<-> is the distance, 1 - similarity. ORDER BY distance LIMIT 1 is a "did you mean" lookup; name breaks ties. A GiST trigram index can return rows in this order directly, GIN can't.

IZMIR finds İzmir at 1.00, because pg_trgm lowercases with the database's rules (C.UTF-8 maps I and İ to i). Turkish letters are another matter: sanliurfa reaches only 0.25, below the % threshold; igdir lands on İzmir (0.20) rather than Iğdır; ızmır, which is what Turkish lowercasing makes of IZMIR, shares almost nothing with İzmir.

examples.title: A folded search key: unaccent in an IMMUTABLE wrapper, under a trigram index

annotations.note: unaccent replaces characters by a rules table (unaccent.rules): ş to s, ı to i, İ to I, ğ to g. In Turkish these are letters of their own, not accented ones; the table doesn't care, which is exactly what input typed on an English keyboard needs.

unaccent is STABLE and index expressions need IMMUTABLE, hence the wrapper; IMMUTABLE is our promise to reindex if unaccent.rules ever changes. The RETURN body (SQL-standard, PG 14) is parsed now and records its dependencies. A quoted body would be parsed at run time, and since PG 17 CREATE INDEX, REINDEX and ANALYZE run with a safe search_path: tested here, such a wrapper fails with 'text search dictionary "unaccent" does not exist'.

10,000 generated village names give the planner a reason to use the index. The index stores the trigrams of search_key(name): every I variant (I, ı, İ, i) becomes i, and ş, ğ, ç, ö, ü lose their marks.
Every ASCII spelling now finds its city at 1.00, and ızmır meets İzmir. Istambul still scores 0.50: folding fixes letters, trigrams fix typos, and the two combine.
search_key('SANLIURFA') is computed once at plan time, and search_key(name) is exactly the indexed expression, so the GIN index answers %. A query spelled lower(unaccent(name)) wouldn't match it.
The price: kır (countryside) and kir (dirt), ılık (lukewarm) and ilik (bone marrow) share a key. Use the key to find candidates; display, rank and compare with the original text.
Indexing unaccent directly fails: functions in an index expression must be IMMUTABLE (SQLSTATE 42P17).

examples.title: Nondeterministic ICU collations: Turkish case-insensitive =, LIKE and UNIQUE

annotations.note: ks-level2 compares letters and accents but ignores case; ks-level1 ignores accents too. tr uses the Turkish case pairs (I/ı, İ/i) and treats ç, ğ, ı, ö, ş and ü as letters of their own; und, the root locale, uses Unicode's defaults. deterministic = false is what allows different strings to compare equal.

tr_ci pairs ISPARTA with ısparta and İZMİR with izmir, but not IZMIR with izmir. und_ci does the opposite: I pairs with i, and İ counts as I with a dot accent, equal to i only at level 1. Çeşme equals cesme only under und_ai, because Turkish treats ç and ş as letters at every level. Iğdır never equals igdir: even the root collation keeps ı apart. No collation is the folded key of the previous example.

On the column, the collation makes every comparison Turkish and case-insensitive, with no lower() in the queries, and the primary key index follows it. citext would apply the database's lower() instead, which maps I to i.
IŞIK finds ışık. LIKE with a nondeterministic collation is new in PG 18; ILIKE, SIMILAR TO and regular expressions still refuse such collations (ILIKE fails with SQLSTATE 0A000).
The primary key compares with the column's collation, so DENİZ is a duplicate of Deniz: case variants can't register as separate users.

use_cases: "Did you mean": the nearest city, product or customer name to a misspelled query (ORDER BY name <-> $1 LIMIT 5)
Search boxes used from English keyboards or phones without Turkish letters: igdir, sanliurfa, IZMIR
Case-insensitive identities with Turkish rules: usernames, tags, city names in a UNIQUE column
Substring search (LIKE '%fragment%') on titles and codes, with a trigram index
strengths: Typo tolerance with no external engine: similarity, % and <-> work per row and are indexable with GIN or GiST
unaccent folds Turkish letters that Unicode normalization keeps: ı has no decomposition, so Python's NFKD trick leaves it alone; unaccent maps it to i
A nondeterministic collation moves case-insensitivity into the schema: =, LIKE (PG 18), UNIQUE and the index agree, and no query can forget a lower()
weaknesses: Trigram similarity knows nothing about language: ş and s, ı and i are simply different characters, so ASCII-typed Turkish scores low without folding
unaccent is STABLE: indexing it needs an IMMUTABLE wrapper, a promise Postgres doesn't check
Folding merges distinct Turkish words (kır and kir)
Nondeterministic collations cost performance, rule out B-tree deduplication, and don't support ILIKE, SIMILAR TO or regular expressions

pitfalls.title: pg_trgm on a database with LC_CTYPE C
pitfalls.detail: pg_trgm decides which characters are letters through the database's LC_CTYPE, fixed at CREATE DATABASE. Before StackLab's playground database was recreated, it had LC_CTYPE C, and show_trgm('ığdır') returned only {"  d","  r"," d "," r "}: ı and ğ counted as separators, weakening similarity and trigram index lookups on Turkish words. Run show_trgm('ığdır') on a new server: six entries is right. Fixing it means a new database; scripts/fix-playground-ctype.sql does that for the playground.

pitfalls.title: Indexing unaccent() directly
pitfalls.detail: unaccent is STABLE, so CREATE INDEX fails with 'functions in index expression must be marked IMMUTABLE'. Wrap it, and use the wrapper in both the index and the queries.
pitfalls.bad: CREATE INDEX ON places USING gin (lower(unaccent(name)) gin_trgm_ops);
pitfalls.good: CREATE INDEX ON places USING gin (search_key(name) gin_trgm_ops);

pitfalls.title: A wrapper whose body is a string
pitfalls.detail: Since PG 17, CREATE INDEX, REINDEX, ANALYZE and VACUUM run with a safe search_path, so a quoted body can't find an unaccent installed in another schema: 'text search dictionary "unaccent" does not exist'. Use a RETURN body, which is parsed when the function is created, or schema-qualify the function and the dictionary.
pitfalls.bad: CREATE FUNCTION search_key(text) RETURNS text LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE AS 'SELECT lower(unaccent(''unaccent''::regdictionary, $1))';
pitfalls.good: CREATE FUNCTION search_key(text) RETURNS text LANGUAGE sql IMMUTABLE PARALLEL SAFE STRICT RETURN lower(unaccent('unaccent'::regdictionary, $1));

pitfalls.title: Expecting an accent-insensitive collation to fold Turkish letters
pitfalls.detail: und-u-ks-level1 equates Çeşme with cesme but keeps ı apart from i; tr-u-ks-level1 equates neither, because in Turkish they are letters. For users typing without Turkish letters, compare folded keys instead.

pitfalls.title: ILIKE on a nondeterministic column
pitfalls.detail: ILIKE doesn't support nondeterministic collations and fails with SQLSTATE 0A000. Since PG 18, plain LIKE does, and it is already case-insensitive under such a collation.
pitfalls.bad: SELECT username FROM users WHERE username ILIKE 'den%';
pitfalls.good: SELECT username FROM users WHERE username LIKE 'den%';

quiz.q: Why does sanliurfa score only 0.25 against Şanlıurfa?
options: ş and ı are different characters from s and i, so most trigrams differ
The similarity threshold is set too low
quiz.why: pg_trgm lowercases but doesn't fold letters; folding both sides with unaccent makes them identical.

quiz.q: CREATE INDEX ... USING gin (lower(unaccent(name)) gin_trgm_ops) fails. Why?
options: unaccent is STABLE, and index expressions need IMMUTABLE functions
Only a superuser may index unaccent
quiz.why: unaccent depends on a dictionary that could change. An IMMUTABLE wrapper is the accepted workaround, with the duty to reindex if the rules change.

quiz.q: Under a nondeterministic collation with locale tr-u-ks-level2, which pair compares equal?
quiz.why: Turkish case pairs are I/ı and İ/i; level 2 still distinguishes accents, and in Turkish ç and ş are separate letters anyway.

quiz.q: username text COLLATE tr_ci (nondeterministic). What does WHERE username ILIKE 'den%' do on PG 18?
options: Raises an error: ILIKE doesn't support nondeterministic collations
quiz.why: PG 18 added LIKE support for nondeterministic collations, not ILIKE. Use LIKE, which is case-insensitive under this collation.

PostgreSQL docs: CREATE FUNCTION (SQL-standard function bodies)

body:
## Concept

Full-text search matches words. People also expect a search box to forgive two other
things, and Postgres has a tool for each, plus one for case:

- **Typos:** `pg_trgm` cuts strings into trigrams and measures their overlap.
  `similarity()` gives a score, `%` tests it against a threshold, `<->` is the distance
  for "did you mean" ordering, and GIN or GiST trigram indexes serve `%`, `LIKE`, `ILIKE`
  and regular expressions.
- **Letters typed differently:** `unaccent` maps characters through a rules table, so
  *sanliurfa* and *Şanlıurfa* get the same key. It is STABLE, so indexing it takes an
  IMMUTABLE wrapper.
- **Case:** a nondeterministic ICU collation such as `tr-u-ks-level2` makes `=`, `LIKE`
  (PG 18), `UNIQUE` and indexes ignore case, with Turkish case pairs.

The Turkish angle is that people write *Iğdır* at least three ways: *Iğdır*, *IĞDIR*
and *igdir*. A collation handles case, trigrams handle typos, and only a folded key
handles a keyboard without Turkish letters. `pg_trgm` itself lowercases with the
database's rules (`C.UTF-8` here, I to i), and decides what counts as a letter through
the database's `LC_CTYPE`.

## Coming from C/C++/Java/Python/JS

- **Python:** `similarity` is in the spirit of `difflib.SequenceMatcher.ratio()`, but
  computed next to the data and indexable. The usual accent strip,
  `unicodedata.normalize('NFKD', s)` followed by dropping combining marks, turns ş into s
  but leaves ı alone (ı has no decomposition); `unaccent`'s table maps it to i.
- **Java:** a `Collator` for `Locale.forLanguageTag("tr")` with strength `SECONDARY` is
  `tr-u-ks-level2`; `PRIMARY` is level 1. Postgres applies the same idea (with ICU's
  rules) to `=`, `UNIQUE` and indexes rather than only to `compare()`.
- **JS:** `new Intl.Collator('tr', { sensitivity: 'accent' })` corresponds to
  `tr-u-ks-level2`, and `sensitivity: 'base'` to level 1.
- **Go:** `golang.org/x/text/collate` with `language.Turkish` and `collate.IgnoreCase`
  gives the same comparisons in application code.

## Design notes

Pick the tool by the job:

- **Display and sort:** the original text, ordered with `COLLATE "tr-x-icu"`.
- **Identity and uniqueness** (usernames, tags): a nondeterministic Turkish collation on
  the column. The citext docs themselves recommend nondeterministic collations over
  citext, which lowercases with the database's rules and so pairs I with i.
- **Finding:** a folded key (`lower(unaccent(...))` in an IMMUTABLE wrapper) with a
  trigram index, matched with `%` or `LIKE`. Store it as a generated column
  (`name_key text GENERATED ALWAYS AS (search_key(name)) STORED`) if many queries use it.
- **Words in prose:** full-text search with the `turkish` configuration. The pg_trgm docs
  suggest combining the two: collect the words of your documents with
  `ts_stat('SELECT to_tsvector(''simple'', body) FROM ...')`, index that word list with
  trigrams, and offer the nearest word when a search finds nothing.

**GIN or GiST.** Both serve filtering (`%`, `LIKE`, `ILIKE`, regex). Choose GiST when
you need `ORDER BY name <-> $1 LIMIT n` served from the index: the docs note that GIN
can't return rows by distance.

**Thresholds are per session.** `%` uses `pg_trgm.similarity_threshold` (0.3). Short
strings have few trigrams, so one typo moves their score a lot; test the threshold on
your real names, or order by `<->` with a `LIMIT` instead of filtering with `%`.

**casefold() isn't the Turkish answer either.** PG 18's `casefold()` follows the
collation: under this database's `C.UTF-8` it leaves İ as it is (`dİyarbakir`), with
`COLLATE "tr-x-icu"` it gives `diyarbakır`. For Turkish text, the collation decides.

**Letters come from LC_CTYPE, not the collation.** The pg_trgm docs don't say how it
finds words; the source does. Its letter test (contrib/pg_trgm/trgm.h, macro ISWORDCHR)
calls `t_isalnum_with_len` (src/backend/tsearch/ts_locale.c), which asks the C library
under the database's LC_CTYPE, whatever the collation provider; when LC_CTYPE is C it
tests single bytes, so every non-ASCII letter is a separator. Observed on PostgreSQL 18.7
here: `show_trgm('ığdır')` has six trigrams under today's LC_CTYPE 'English_United
States.1252', and had four, only those of d and r, under the playground's earlier
LC_CTYPE 'C' (the pitfall). What PostgreSQL 18 moved to the collation provider is
lower-casing: its release notes name pg_trgm under the change to full text search, and
contrib/pg_trgm/trgm_op.c now lower-cases with `str_tolower` and the default collation
where 17 used libc. On another server, check `datctype` in `pg_database`.
